message.content:
In Texas, tenants have a number of statutory rights designed to protect them from unfair treatment and ensure safe, habitable living conditions. Below is an overview of key tenant rights under Texas law (Texas Property Code, Chapter 24) and related statutes: | Category | Key Rights | Practical Implications | |----------|------------|------------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months’ rent for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within 30 days after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | • Keep records of the deposit amount and any receipts. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, and pest control.
• Must keep the premises in a condition fit for habitation. | • Report problems promptly; document with photos or written notices. | | **Repair & Deduct / Rent Withhold** | • If landlord fails to repair after notice, tenant may pay for repairs and deduct cost from rent, or withhold rent until repairs are made. | • Keep receipts and provide written notice to landlord before withholding. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑payment of rent: 3‑day notice to pay or vacate.
• For lease termination: 30‑day notice if lease is month‑to‑month; 60‑day notice for longer leases.
• For entry: 48‑hour written notice for non‑emergency visits. | • Provide notice in writing (email, text, or letter). | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlord cannot enter without proper notice unless emergency. | • Landlord must respect your right to quiet enjoyment. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Protected classes: race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, etc. | • Landlords cannot refuse or discriminate based on these factors. | | **Lease Terms** | • Lease must be in writing if it lasts longer than one year.
• Must include rent amount, security deposit, lease term, and contact info. | • Review lease carefully before signing. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow court procedures: serve notice, file complaint, attend hearing. | • Tenants can contest eviction in court. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has no statewide rent control; landlords set rent freely. | • However, local ordinances may impose limits in certain cities. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide hot water, electricity, and gas. | • If utilities fail, you may withhold rent or seek court order. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Tenant may sublet only with landlord’s consent, which cannot be unreasonably withheld. | • Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Maintenance of Common Areas** | • Landlord responsible for common areas (hallways, elevators, etc.). | • Report issues promptly. | | **Legal Remedies** | • Tenants can sue for breach of contract, damages, or unlawful eviction. | • Keep documentation of all interactions. | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of lease, receipts, emails, texts, and photos of any damage or maintenance issues. 2. **Use Written Notices** – Send notices via certified mail or email with read receipt to establish proof. 3. **Know the Timeline** – Understand how many days’ notice are required for each situation. 4. **Seek Legal Advice** – If disputes arise, consult a lawyer or tenant advocacy group (e.g., Texas Tenants Union). 5. **File Complaints** – If landlord violates health or safety codes, report to local housing authority or the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs. ### Resources - **Texas Property Code** – Chapter 24 (Landlord‑Tenant Law) - **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** – Provides consumer guides on rental agreements. - **Local Housing Authorities** – For city-specific ordinances or assistance programs. - **Legal Aid Organizations** – e.g., Texas Legal Services Center, local bar association referral services. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general in nature and not legal advice. For specific situations, consult a licensed attorney familiar with Texas landlord‑tenant law.
